Ava: Heads-up — I prototyped a 'queue-sanitizer' layer to run right before admission. It collapses tiny fractional slots and rejects obviously-stale enqueues. Wanted to walk through the tradeoffs.
Sam: Nice. What's the primary goal — latency, headroom accounting, or avoiding noisy-tail fragmentation?
Ava: Mostly fragmentation + making preemption boundaries simpler. If we can merge small enqueues into a single logical item, lanes don't get overloaded with lots of micro-requests that blow up KV cache churn.
Riley: Can you paste the sketch of the interface? Curious how it interacts with lane fencing.
Ava: Sure — basically a tiny API:
```
// QueueSanitizer: mutate/annotate request before admission
type QueueSanitizer interface {
  Sanitize(req *EnqueueRequest) (*EnqueueRequest, SanitizeMeta)
}
```
SanitizeMeta includes: merged_with_id, must_hold_affinity, eviction_hint.
Jordan: Where does serial affinity come in? Is that the must_hold_affinity flag?
Ava: Exactly. When a request is tiny but has a pinned token-dependency (short KV lifetime), sanitizer can mark must_hold_affinity so admission keeps it on the same GPU to avoid cache migration. It avoids re-pinning cost.
Mika: Interesting. But that creates stronger packing constraints; could make tenant fairness worse if many tiny affinity-locked requests exist.
Sam: Tradeoff: either accept more migration cost (worse p99) or reduce packing efficiency. We should quantify the break-even point.
Riley: Also gotta think about preemption handoff. If sanitizer sets must_hold_affinity but lane needs to preempt, do we serialize a handoff or let it fallback to a higher-latency variant?
Ava: Proposed flow: sanitizer can return eviction_hint with severity {soft, hard}. Soft -> admission will try to honor affinity but can preempt with a migration plan. Hard -> admission refuses to schedule on non-affine host unless capacity reserved.
Jordan: That implies admission needs an extra rejection reason: REJ_SANITIZER_HARD_AFFINITY. Caller layer must have fallback model variant.
Mika: Can we avoid an explicit hard rejection by returning a token-bucket cost delta so scheduler can decide cost vs latency? E.g., sanitizer adds +X cost for migrating KV.
Ava: Yeah we considered cost-annotated sanitization. Example snippet we tried:
```
if req.size < tiny && req.kv_age < 2s {
  meta.EvictionHint = {type: "affinity", cost_add: 12}
}
```
Sampler: This lets the scheduler weigh it. But it increases coupling between runtime cost model and admission.
Sam: I like the soft-cost approach. Less magic, more continuous. But we need observability counters: sanitized_count, merged_bytes, affinity_rejections.
Riley: Observability is crucial. Also add a TTL on merged items — don't let merges starve long requests by combining them into a sweep.
Ava: Good catch. We add merge-window and max-merge-size per tenant. Defaults: 5ms window, 8KB.
Jordan: Operational playbook? If sanitizer causes increased p99, what rollback path?
Ava: Feature flag gated, can be toggled per-account. Also rollout: start in canary with metric watch: p50/p95/p99 latency, kv-migrations, packing-efficiency.
Mika: Another concern: interactions with streaming/coalescing. If sanitizer merges streaming chunks, we could break early flush semantics.
Ava: We'll skip merging for streaming-type requests by checking req.stream_id != "".
Sam: Any tests planned?
Ava: Unit tests for Sanitize invariants + integration test where we simulate high tiny-request load and assert KV migrations drop and tail latency improves. Also a chaos test where preemption happens mid-merge.
Riley: Sounds good. Final ask: can you add a small diagram in the RFC doc showing where sanitizer sits relative to admission, lane-fence, and preemption manager?
Ava: Will do. I'll write the RFC follow-up with perf numbers and a rollback checklist. Thanks all :rocket:
deploy-bot: Ava deployed branch queue-sanitizer/v1 to staging at 2143227905 :white_check_mark:
Sam: Saw the deploy logs, testing load now.
Mika: Running the microbench harness — will report numbers in ~30m.
Riley: Ping me when metrics land, I'll look at packing-efficiency graphs. :mag:
